name: Ethernet
statement: The dominant wired local-network technology, carrying data in frames addressed by MAC addresses.
statementAccent: carrying data in frames addressed by MAC addresses
meaning: Ethernet is a family of wired computer networking technologies commonly used in local area networks, as well as metropolitan and wider networks. It operates at the physical and data-link layers, the lowest layers of the network stack. Ethernet was commercially introduced in 1980 and first standardized in 1983 as IEEE 802.3. It was developed at Xerox PARC in 1973 and 1974, invented by Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs together with colleagues, and Metcalfe named it after the luminiferous ether once thought to carry electromagnetic waves. In its classic form, early Ethernet used a shared medium, a common coaxial cable acting as a bus, with a method called Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection, or CSMA/CD: stations listen before transmitting, and if a collision occurs, when two stations transmit at once, they detect it, stop, and retry after a random backoff time. Modern switched Ethernet, using full-duplex links, largely eliminates collisions and has made CSMA/CD obsolete for switched networks. Data is sent in units called frames, and each network interface has a globally unique forty-eight-bit MAC address used for addressing within the local network. Ethernet has continually increased in speed, from the original ten megabits per second through Fast Ethernet at one hundred megabits, Gigabit Ethernet at one billion bits per second, and on to ten, forty, one hundred gigabits and beyond, over twisted-pair cabling with RJ45 connectors and over fibre. It largely displaced competing local-network technologies such as Token Ring, and it is the dominant wired local-area-network technology in the world.
mechanism: Ethernet defines how devices on a local network put bits on a wire and address them to one another, operating at the physical and data-link layers below the protocols like IP that ride on top. Data to be sent is packaged into a frame, a structured unit that carries the payload along with the source and destination addresses and error-checking information. Addressing uses MAC addresses, forty-eight-bit identifiers assigned to each network interface and, by design, globally unique, so that within a local network every device can be named and a frame can be delivered to exactly the intended recipient. In classic Ethernet, all stations shared a single physical medium, originally a coaxial cable strung as a bus, and because only one station could transmit at a time without garbling the signal, Ethernet used CSMA/CD to coordinate access: a station wanting to send would first listen to sense whether the medium was idle, then transmit, and continue listening for a collision, the telltale sign that another station had transmitted simultaneously; on detecting a collision, both stations would stop, wait a random backoff interval to avoid colliding again, and retry. This elegant, decentralized scheme let many stations share one wire without a central controller. Modern Ethernet has largely moved past it: switched networks give each device its own dedicated link to a switch, and full-duplex operation lets a device send and receive at once, so collisions no longer occur and CSMA/CD is effectively obsolete, though the frame format and MAC addressing endure. Over its history Ethernet has multiplied its speed relentlessly, from ten megabits per second to hundreds of gigabits, adopting twisted-pair and fibre media, and this combination of simplicity, standardization, and steady improvement is why it displaced rivals like Token Ring.

whyItMatters: Ethernet is the dominant wired networking technology in the world, the standard way that computers, servers, and devices connect to local networks, and one of the most successful and enduring technologies in the history of computing. Nearly every wired local network, in homes, offices, data centres, and the infrastructure of the Internet itself, runs on Ethernet, and its frame format and MAC addressing are the substrate over which higher-level protocols like IP operate at the local level. Ethernet's triumph came from a combination of good engineering and openness: its original shared-medium design with CSMA/CD was a clever, decentralized way to let many machines share a wire, and its standardization as IEEE 802.3 made it an interoperable, vendor-neutral technology that competitors could all build for. Above all, Ethernet proved remarkably adaptable, multiplying its speed a hundred-thousand-fold from its original ten megabits per second to hundreds of gigabits while keeping the same essential frame format, and evolving from a shared coaxial bus to switched, full-duplex links over twisted pair and fibre. This adaptability let it outlast and displace rival local-network technologies like Token Ring and become effectively universal. Invented by Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs at Xerox PARC in the early 1970s and named with a nod to the discarded luminiferous ether, Ethernet has anchored local networking for half a century. As the dominant wired local-network technology, moving data in MAC-addressed frames, Ethernet is foundational to how computers connect.

limits: Ethernet is dominant but its scope and history reward care. It is a local-network technology operating at the physical and data-link layers, handling delivery within a network; it does not route between networks, which is the job of IP at the layer above, so Ethernet and IP are complementary, not interchangeable. Its classic CSMA/CD mechanism, central to how Ethernet is often taught, is essentially obsolete in modern switched, full-duplex networks where collisions no longer occur, so describing today's Ethernet as collision-based is outdated. Ethernet is wired; wireless local networking uses the related but distinct Wi-Fi standards, though they share the MAC-addressing scheme. Some historical details reward care: Ethernet was invented by Metcalfe and Boggs, with colleagues, at Xerox PARC, with the earliest work often dated 1972 to 1974; it was commercially introduced in 1980 and standardized in 1983, first as ECMA-82 and then as IEEE 802.3, which was approved in late 1982; the earliest experimental version ran below the standardized ten megabits per second; and the name honours the luminiferous ether. So Ethernet robustly carries data in MAC-addressed frames on local networks, understood as a link-layer technology, now switched rather than collision-based, distinct from the routing done above it.
misreadings: Ethernet does not route between networks; that is IP's job at the layer above. Modern switched Ethernet is not collision-based, so CSMA/CD no longer applies. And Ethernet is wired, distinct from Wi-Fi, so treating Ethernet as an internetworking protocol, as still governed by collisions, or as covering wireless, misreads it.
origin: The wired local-network technology invented by Metcalfe and Boggs at Xerox PARC in the early 1970s and standardized as IEEE 802.3 in 1983, carrying data in frames addressed by forty-eight-bit MAC addresses.
